utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-9-PT, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the appearances. MR. DI FAZIO: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. DE FAZIO: I appear for the Prosecution together with my learned friend Ms. Reidy, who is on my right. On my left is Diane Boles, who is the case manager in this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Igor Pantelic Defence counsel on behalf of Mr. Blagoje Simic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Ms. Catherine Baen for Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Novak Lukic for Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour my name is Borislav Pisarevic on behalf of the defence of Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There are a number of matters which we have to raise and consider, and in respect of some of them, make a decision on for this Pre-Trial Conference. The first matter that I have concerns the Prosecution, and it is that the Chamber observes that you have only one charge in Count 3, under Article 2. That's the grave breach charge. You have, apparently, withdrawn all the other grave breach charges. Now, in light of the fact that the same conduct which is the subject matter of the grave breach Article 2 charge is also the subject matter of another charge under Article 5, crimes against humanity, the question arises, firstly, whether or, rather, why you have retained this single charge and whether in light of the fact that the same conduct is the subject matter of another charge, whether you would not wish to consider either dropping the grave breach charge or if you decide to keep it, then to drop the charge under Article 5 in respect of crimes against humanity. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour. Do I understand the Tribunal to -- the Chamber to want a response from me on this matter right now? Because naturally I would prefer to consider my position before addressing the Chamber on the matter. It catches me somewhat by surprise. I didn't expect to have to deal with this issue this afternoon, and I would prefer to be able to consider the matter and take counsel with my colleagues on the issue. I'm sure that if the Chamber were minded to grant me some time, I could provide a response within a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. The Chamber will give you a week in which to provide a response on this. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm grateful to the Chamber. I have noted the comments and I will make sure the matter is attended to swiftly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You might want to look at the Krnojelac case in which the same issue arose. And when it was brought to the attention of the Prosecutor, they decided to withdraw the grave breach charge. Of course you're not obliged to do that. But another matter for you to consider is the recent development in the Tribunal's jurisprudence relating to cumulative charges, because it is likely that in any event, in the -- ultimately it would be one or the other. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand the comments of the Chamber and with respect, I think it's an entirely appropriate matter to address now at this point, and I have no trouble with providing a response within a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: The only other that matter perhaps I should raise is the method of that response. Does the Chamber envisage a motion or some other method of communication of my view or the Prosecution's view on this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It would be by way of a written response to the Chamber's comments on this matter. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next matter relates to Blagoje Simic, and here I'd like to speak to the counsel for Mr. Blagoje Simic. I observe, Mr. Pantelic, that in the joint statement of facts in respect of which there was a stipulation by both the Prosecution and the Defence, this was filed on the 27th of April. It is stated that Blagoje Simic was and here I quote: "From the 4th November 1991, through at least the 30th of November 1992, was the deputy of the assembly of the self-declared Serb autonomous region of Northern Bosnia." End of quotation. But we observed in the pre-trial brief filed by Mr Simic that he takes the position that he was not the deputy president of the -- yes. I'm sorry. I was saying that I observe that in his pre-trial brief, Mr Simic takes the position that he was not the deputy president of the assembly of the Serb autonomous region of Northern Bosnia. The purpose of these joint statements is to limit the number of issues by way of agreement, and if you have -- if you have already agreed, as a matter of fact, that he was the president, it is incomprehensible that in the pre-trial brief it should be argued that he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will give you the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will try to give you an answer. In fact, the further document that you are referring to is the document, I suppose, from, I think, several years ago, 13th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 1992, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I discussed this issue with the -- with the -- my client, and it's obviously probably some error in process of discussion with the Prosecutor's office. So that was the case in filing the joint statement dated April 27th. After that, during the conversation with my client and conference related to clarification of certain facts and issues, the position of Blagoje Simic was that -- I mean according to the result of our conversation, that he was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So it's just a matter of timing. Because we were not able to discuss this matter, this issue, prior to our pre-trial brief. It was by the end of April when we discussed this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's something for the Prosecutor to note, but it -- the Chamber did see that apparent inconsistency. So the trial will then proceed on the basis that he was not the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. That would be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I turn next to the question of exhibits, and it's a matter now for the Prosecutor. Mr. Di Fazio, the Prosecution has provided a list of 213 exhibits, divided into seven categories, but nothing has been made to link the various exhibits to the charges in the indictment, and this is, in fact, required by the Rules. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Yes. I take Your Honour's point. Your Honours are concerned to have some sort of document or linkage between each individual item on the exhibit list, whether it be a document or a map or whatever, and its relevance to a particular portion of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Precisely. Precisely. The whole idea is to facilitate the trial process. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Well, I regret that has not been done, if Your Honours please, and if you wish me, and I take it you do wish me to prepare such a document, again it's something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we actually require you to do it because the rules require it. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And we'll give you a time period of 28 days -- MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- in which to do this. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'm grateful to the Chamber. I'm sure that that can be accomplished easily in that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the same thing can be done in respect of the documents which have been admitted by way of pre-trial admission. There are 129 documents, including transcripts of interviews with the accused, and these were admitted without objection from the Defence, and again, these should be linked to the charges. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So if you would see that that is done as well. MR. DI FAZIO: That, of course, can be done. In respect of the interviews, would the Chamber like an analysis, essentially, of each interview and the matter to which it relates in the indictment? Is that the sort of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That would be helpful, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Of course that will be attended to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Again now, Mr. Di Fazio, the question of protective measures. Protective measures were granted in respect of eight witnesses, witnesses A to C and E to I. At the Status Conference on the 15th of May of this year, you told us that one of the protected witnesses, Witness I, would not be called. Only two of the protective witnesses now appear on the main witness list, that is, Witnesses A, number 34, and G, number 35. Three protected witnesses, Witnesses C, E, and F, appear on the reserve list but there is no mention of Witnesses B and H, and the Chamber assumes from this that these two witnesses will not be called. MR. DI FAZIO: May I just consult my exhibit -- sorry, my witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: The assumptions was that which witnesses would not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: B and H, because they are not mentioned on the reserve list at all. MR. DI FAZIO: No. They're not on the Prosecution's witness list, and we don't intend to call them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To call them. Thank you. Again, Mr. Di Fazio, the next issue relates to witnesses whose evidence may be cumulative. The Chamber did an analysis of the evidence of the witnesses, and we have found 13 witnesses whose evidence may qualify as being cumulative. MR. DI FAZIO: May I just ask Your Honour at this point, when you say cumulative, do you essentially mean repetitive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I mean repetitive. Yes, I mean repetitive. I'm going to read out fairly slowly the witnesses and the evidence. What the Chamber proposes to do is not to take a decision now as to the deletion of these witnesses but merely to bring the matter to your attention so that you can consider it, and we would give you a time period of two weeks in which to report back to us the result of your examination. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will read out the witnesses and just a very brief summary of the evidence which is cumulative, repetitive. The first is Witness number 3. She addresses the treatment of non-Serbs after the take-over, question of looting, an attack on the mosque, expulsion from home, forced transfer of assets, arrest and beatings of husband, events at the TO building, forced labour, and the attendance of the accused Zaric at meetings and the involvement of Tadic in exchanges and expulsion. Then Witness number 4, a doctor who addresses the condition of detainees in various locations and involvement of Tadic in exchanges and expulsion. You don't have to write them down because I will have the senior legal officer hand you what I am reading. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I am grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness number 7, a Muslim male who can testify as to the takeover of Bosanski Samac, the treatment of non-Serbs afterwards, the involvement of Tadic and Zaric in looting, forced labour, and involvement of Tadic in exchanges, expulsion. Number 8 is a woman who can testify as to the treatment of non-Serbs, the arrest of her son, the involvement of Tadic and Zaric in looting, and the involvement of Tadic in exchanges and expulsion. Number 10 is a female teacher who will testify as to the treatment of non-Serbs, the appropriation of assets, the involvement of Zaric in forced labour, and the involvement of Tadic in exchanges and expulsion. Number 11 is a woman who will testify or who can testify as to the treatment of non-Serbs, arrests, forced labour, expulsion from home, and the involvement of Tadic in exchanges and expulsion. Number 16, a Bosnian Muslim mobilised into the Serb army. He will address issues of forced labour, detention, and the involvement of Zaric in the army. Number 18, an elderly woman who can address the arrest and detention of her husband, destruction of local mosque, involvement of Zaric in forced labour, and involvement of Tadic in exchanges and expulsion. Number 19 is a widow who can testify as to the treatment of non-Serbs, looting, forced labour, and expulsion from home, the involvement of Tadic in searching for weapons. Number 26 observed meetings of the 4th Detachment at Tadic's cafe attended by Zaric, was arrested, and can testify as to the involvement of Tadic in exchanges and/or expulsion. Number 30, Bosnian Muslim married to a Bosnian Croat, can testify as to the takeover of Bosanski Samac, involvement of Tadic and Zaric in search of apartment for weapons, arrest and detention, involvement of Tadic in exchanges and expulsion. And number 33, a Muslim drafted into the Serb army, who is in a position to testify as to forced labour, looting, and the role of Zaric. Those are the 13 witnesses whose evidence may be cumulative. You should examine their testimony and report back to us in two weeks as to whether they will be retained on the list. The next issue again concerns you, Mr. Di Fazio. You have listed two investigators as potential witnesses, numbers 36 and 37. These investigators will give evidence of interviews with witnesses, collection of documents, and other general matters. The Chamber takes the view that it's not necessary to have these investigators testify. Accordingly, we will order that their names be deleted from the witness list. Next, on your reserve witness list, which has 15 witnesses, we observe that most of the witnesses address general issues, but there is one, number 40, a major in the TO, the territorial army, he is in a position to provide direct evidence as to the role of one of the accused and some limited evidence related to another. The Chamber's position is that this person should actually testify, and so we will, in exercise of the powers we have under the Rules, require that this person be listed as a witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, in relation to the reserve witnesses, all but two of the reserve witnesses have some direct knowledge of the activities of the accused. Those are numbers 48 and 50. Now, those two could either be removed from the list on the basis that they're not necessary for -- that their testimony is not necessary for the proceedings, or if the view is taken that their testimony is necessary, then their testimony could be let in by way of Rule 92 bis. That's numbers 48 and 50. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, because they don't go directly to the acts of the accused. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But what would your position be then, that they would -- their evidence could be adduced by way of Rule 92 bis? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or you would want their evidence to be in? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, the position at this stage, bear in mind, Your Honours, that I'm hearing what you say now for the first time, but my position at this stage is that we would want their evidence in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: But I'm mindful of what the Chamber has said, and of course I would review the evidence of those two particular witnesses, bearing in mind the comments that you've made with respect to the other witnesses in the spirit -- and in a spirit of trying to cut down the witness list wherever possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. The next matter again concerns the Prosecution. On the 20th of June, we had required that the Office of the Prosecutor disclose all interviews with Mr. Todorovic to the Defence. Can you say whether those disclosures have been made? MR. DI FAZIO: This has been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Has been done. Yes. There is a motion that was filed recently by the Prosecutor to have the expert testimony of Mr. Donia. We grant this motion. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is also a motion filed recently by the Prosecutor for the admission of transcripts. We can't dispose of that now, but two issues arise. In paragraph 5 of your motion, you say that the basis of the motion is that it is in support of this adjudicated fact. The reference here is to the question of the international status of the armed conflict, and you refer in paragraph 4 to evidence in two other cases, Tadic and Celebici. It's not clear to the Chamber whether you're using the term adjudicated fact there as a term of art, because if it is an adjudicated fact, then there is a procedure, a discreet procedure under the Rules for the reception of adjudicated facts, in Rule 94, and for that reason, you will not need to utilise the procedure for transcripts under Rule 92 bis. So I'm not clear whether the term "adjudicated facts" there was used very loosely. MR. DI FAZIO: I think it can only be read as a loose -- in a loose sense. It would read just as well in support of this alleged fact. In fact, this matter has a history going back to 1998 in this case, when a motion was laid before the Court seeking precisely that the Court take judicial notice or accept as an adjudicated fact that there was an international armed conflict at the relevant times in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Trial Chamber declined to make such an order. Subsequently there was the appeal, the appeals, I should say, in both Celebici and Tadic in which that issue was commented upon. But I think the position of the Prosecution has to be here that this is an alleged fact and something that the Prosecution seeks to prove and seeks to prove through the admission of this material that's the subject of the 92 bis motion. So it's not really used in the sense of -- as a term of art.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. In that case then, in the light of that clarification, what remains for us to do is to set a date for the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The hearing will be on Wednesday, the 25th, p.m. That's at 2.30, 2.30 p.m. The last matter but perhaps the most important has to do with the duty that the Chamber has under the Rules to fix a time for the presentation of the Prosecution case. I understand, Mr. Di Fazio, that you had estimated a period of eight weeks. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please, given what's transpired this afternoon, it's going to be -- it's going to be very difficult for me to give you any reasonably accurate estimation of trial length particularly because I don't know how many witnesses ultimately I will be calling. What I had done, in an effort to try and get a handle or a fix on the period of time for the Prosecution case, by that I mean evidence in chief and cross-examination, was to go through the list and work out the period of time required for each witness, and using both the lower and the higher estimate that was contained in our witness list that was provided to the Court under Rule 65 ter, I believe it is. And for various reasons that I don't want to go into now, but for various reasons I came up with 47 witnesses. Now I don't know if it's going to be 47 witness because of what -- again I repeat, because of what's been said today. On that basis, on the basis of 47 witnesses, I came up with a figure, and I hope this is not too alarming to the Chamber, on the outer limit of 102 days, sitting days, and this is on the basis of four hours a day, and on the basis of the lower estimate, in the vicinity of 95. Now, if that were to -- if those estimates are anywhere near correct and we do start on September the 10th, that will take us to at least the beginning of January if not to the middle of January, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, experience here in practically every case is that the rate is one witness per day going through the Prosecution. It's very slow, but that seems to be the basis. So on that basis, although it's not clear precisely how many witnesses you're going to call, and although clearly one or two will require more extensive cross-examination and examination-in-chief, nonetheless, there are a number who will, obviously, be quicker. It would seem to be an accurate estimate to say that you will have something in the region of 45 or so witnesses, 40 or so witnesses, perhaps more, perhaps less, and you'll need something like 40 or so days on that basis. MR. DI FAZIO: At -- when Your Honour says a day, do you mean a full sitting day or four hours a day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A day. A day. The fact that you are having four hours isn't much less than the usual sitting day. It's about half an hour less, in fact. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It will be an early start. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I defer to Your Honours' obviously greater experience in these matters than I. That estimate was the best that I could do in the circumstances. If the Chamber takes the view that it is a pessimistic view on my part of the amount of time required, then naturally I take on board what the Chamber says. But if that be the case, then the estimate really depends on the number of witnesses, and would that not be a matter that could be or perhaps should be dealt with once that's crystallized, once we do know for certain how many witness was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What the Chamber had in mind was with the trial starting on the 10th of September, the Prosecution would have ten weeks in which to present its case. So That would take the Prosecution's case to the 16th of November. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I think in the light of Judge May's analysis, that is quite feasible, fairly feasible. Bear in mind, of course, that if events arise which are unforeseen, you can always apply to the Trial Chamber to vary, to extend the time. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful to the Chamber. If the Chamber wishes, I'm happy to provide another estimate after the issue of the full number of witnesses has been crystallised. Your Honour Judge May was quite correct when he said that some of these witnesses will take longer than others. I mentioned it may be of interest to perhaps only one or two counsel or perhaps even only one Defence counsel, in which case the cross-examination will presumably be a lot shorter than the examination-in-chief. The substantial witnesses, however, are probably in the order of about six or seven and may take a little longer than a day. I hear what the Chamber says, and naturally the Prosecution will make every effort to work within that framework, of course, and I'm grateful to the Chamber for pointing out that the Prosecution is at liberty to try to increase the period of time allotted to it if the need arises. I also offer, if it's of assistance, a later estimate perhaps at the next 92 bis motion, or perhaps within the period of time that's been allocated to us to inform the Chamber of our position with respect to the 13 or so witnesses who -- that the Chamber thinks might provide repetitive evidence. After I've settled that, I'm also happy to provide another estimate, if that would be of benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be sensible. So after you've done your analysis, then at the Rule 92 bis hearing on the 25th of July, we can review the position. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I think that would enable the Chamber to -- will certainly enable the Prosecution to forecast whether or not there is going to be any application to increase the amount of time allocated or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are there any matters that the Defence would wish to raise at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I don't think at this time we have something to raise with regard to the procedural matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, on behalf of Mr. Milan Simic, we would like to make a formal request under Rule 68 for the Prosecution to disclose any exculpatory evidence. Apparently the Prosecutors have been great about providing that information in the past, but just for purposes of the record, we would like to make that formal request under the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Also, Your Honours, under Rule 67, the Rule with respect to reciprocal disclosures, the language in the Rule says that -- well, first of all, the Defence and the Prosecution have been in the process of reciprocal disclosure. The language in the Rule says that we are to provide any of this discovery as soon as practicable and before the commencement of trial. And since the Rule is sort of somewhat vague as to when we should disclose this information, we're asking for some guidance from the Court as to when we should comply with this Rule. In other words, when do we have to give it to the Prosecution, within seven days, 14 days? And we would like to request that the Court give us some sort of guidance with respect to this Rule so that we don't have a problem later on when we try to get these matters into evidence and then the Prosecutors may complain that we didn't give it to them as soon as practicable. You understand my request, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. It says "... prior to the commencement of the trial," and the trial date has been fixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. However, we feel that that language might be vague also because at this point we don't know really what's going to happen during the Prosecutor's case. Therefore, if there is some new evidence that comes into our possession that we would like to use when we start our case in chief, we would like to know what the requirements are respect to disclosure to the Office of the Prosecutor. My understanding is we don't have to -- we are not required to tell the Court what evidence we intend to prove at trial until the Defence conference, the pre-Defence conference. Is that correct, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's obviously difficult for the Chamber to determine an issue of this kind in a vacuum. So I don't intend to make a ruling on the point that you have raised. I would, however, indicate that the procedure under Rule 67 is a special procedure, and it's special for a variety of reasons. And if you have an issue which arises in a practical way during the trial, then I think you have to make application and we'll deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We're not trying to create any problem here, we're just trying to show some good faith and avoid problems in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not referring to a special defence at all, an alibi or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no special defence. We're just merely complying with the Rules with respect to reciprocal discovery. If there is some problem in the future, we don't want to be prevented from using that evidence if it is viewed that we are not in compliance with the reciprocal discovery rules, that's all. And we're not trying to create a problem here, we're just trying to be careful, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Rule 67(D) might answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So that does answer the question somewhat. I guess the question is what "promptly notify" means. No one is going to be able to tell that. We'll just do the best we can. Oh, we would like to make a formal request, I guess it's a joint Defence request, that the Prosecutors list the order in which the witnesses will testify and the evidence will be produced. We understand, Your Honours, it's not required by the Rules, but it's my understanding that this practice has happened in other trials and we think it would be a lot easier and make the trial go faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of practice, it is done. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. As I stand here, the attitude of the Prosecution is that, of course, anything to assist, A, the Chamber and the Defence and would also assist the Prosecution as well to have such a list, but I don't want to be bound in -- bound or straitjacketed perhaps is a better word, by any such list. Obviously in any trial there are going to be problems getting witnesses, the order of witnesses, and sticking to it in an absolute sense might eventually cause problems. But I would certainly provide an initial list and one to which the Prosecution will use its best endeavours to stick to in order to provide a guide both to the Chamber and to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's -- I think that's good enough. That's good enough. You provide a list, and as the trial develops, you may have to make changes. This would apply to the Defence, too, when the Defence presents its case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, we have one more issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: As the Court is aware, the Trial Chamber is aware, our client, Mr. Milan Simic, is a paraplegic and has serious medical problems and the Court graciously granted shorter trial days because of the situation. Recently, within the last month or so, Mr. Simic has been examined by his physicians again, and his medical situation may be deteriorating a little bit. We are not filing a motion at this time, but we may be forced, if he gets worse, to file a motion for this Court, based on his physician's examination, to maybe, I hate to say, further shorten the trial days. We hope that's not the case but -- we hope that's not the case, Your Honours, because we want this trial to go as expeditiously as possible, as everyone else does, but if our client gets -- if his medical situation worsens, that we feel we have an obligation to go ahead and present the Court with a motion and the supporting affidavits or information from the physician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have an obligation to act at all times in the best interests of your client.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And I think that's it for the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other matters? Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, there is one matter I want to raise with the Chamber, if I may, and that concerns disclosure. Firstly, I just want to state that as far as the Prosecution is concerned, disclosure has now been completed. This afternoon we will provide about five further statements to the Defence. We have good reason for believing that that material has already been disclosed, but as an abundance -- from an abundance of caution, we'll hand it over again. So generally speaking, disclosure under 66 and 68 has been completed by the Prosecution. There is, however, one matter, and that's the question of reciprocal disclosure under Rule 67. In -- on March the 2nd, 1998, counsel for Mr. Milan Simic, Mr. Simo Zaric, and Mr. Miroslav Tadic wrote to the Office of the Prosecutor seeking, pursuant to Rule 66(B), disclosure. Now, 66(B) refers, as far as I can see, to inspection of documents, photographs, tangible objects, and so on. The issue was briefly raised in one of the Status Conferences in this case later in 1999, but I have been unable to find any orders made consequent upon that request by way of letter. Such a request having been made under 66(B), it seems to me that it triggers 67(C), and the Prosecution is therefore entitled to inspect any books, documents, photographs, and tangible objects which are within the custody or control of the Defence and which it intends to use as evidence at the trial. It may be that much of 67(C) has already been complied with and satisfied. It may be that our rights, the Prosecution's rights under 67(C) have already been satisfied by the simple fact of disclosure, but I need to be satisfied about that completely, I submit, and it's that issue that is concerning me and that I would like to have resolved. I've not been able to find anything in our records indicating that that inspection by the Prosecution of books, documents, photographs, or tangible objects in the possession of those three defendants and which they intend to use at trial has ever been conducted. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment. Is it seems to me that the matter was touched upon at a Status Conference conducted on Friday, the 20th of November, 1998. Now, if the Defence provide the Prosecution with an assurance that such access will be granted or correct me and say that such access has been granted in the past, a matter of which I'm not aware, then of course that would satisfy the Prosecution. I'm not seeking any particular orders, but the exercise of rights under 67 -- 67(C) is a matter that I want to ensure either has been fully conducted or will be conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, as I understand it, you're saying that the Defence made a request of the Prosecutor pursuant to Rule 66(B), and that request has been granted for them to inspect. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Well, they made the request, and as far as I can tell, nothing has ever transpired. Now, I just don't know the reason for that. I can't find anything in the record, if Your Honours please, to indicate that the Prosecution has availed itself of its rights under 67(C), and I therefore believe that it hasn't. And given the distance of that request that was made in 1998, it seems to me that the Prosecution is so entitled, and I'll make it clear for the record that I therefore do wish to inspect -- the Prosecution wishes to inspect any books, documents, photograph, or tangible objects that those three defendants intend to use as evidence at trial. It may be a non-issue. It may be that everything that they have disclosed to us encompasses all of that material, I don't know, but I need to be assured that the Prosecution's rights under that section are fully observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you have been in this case long enough. The Defence did, in fact, request permission to inspect books in the possession of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And that, of course, triggers their right under Rule 67(C) to inspect, books in the custody or control of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is also correct, Your Honour. The thing here is maybe this is a matter of clarification or interpretation. Literally speaking, does it mean that we have to go to your office to inspect tangible objects and the documents, or during the process of reciprocal discovery, you provide with us certain documents? Because if the first solution is reality, it is not done up to now, up to date. We've never been in your office; we've never inspected your archives. But I must admit that through all this process of reciprocal discovery, we will be provided with a certain number of documents from the Prosecutor's side, and I believe that the same will follow from the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I believe this is a matter that has to be settled between the Prosecutor and the Defence, and you must determine the 20 extent to which Rule 67(C) is applicable. If it is applicable and you believe you have a right under it which has not been exercised, then you may make an application. But it seems to me that there are matters to be clarified between the parties, and maybe it's a non-issue. MR. DI FAZIO: That's, with respect, absolutely correct, of course, Your Honour. And I don't want to necessarily create issues. It may be that -- I'm sure that the best way for us to deal with this matter is for me to enter into negotiations or to confer with Defence counsel, and I'm sure that we can both resolve the matter. I felt it appropriate that I should at least raise the issue for the purposes of the record. If I can resolve the issue with Defence counsel, I'm hopeful that we can, that it may be that I don't need to trouble the Chamber again on this the matter. But I just needed to raise it for the purposes of establishing it as a concern. I hope that we will be able to resolve it and that will be the end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There being no other issues, we are adjourned.
